say: Welcome to Challenge Day! Today there is no new topic: there are puzzles from every lesson. Clever inquirers do not always know the answer straight away. They know how to START: draw it, list it, or make a table.
Relay chain: I ask the first question. The answer is the start of the next question, so listen carefully and pass it on. If someone is stuck, the group can help with a hint, not the answer.
Look at the two stations. Which one do you think will be harder? Write your guess, and we will see at the end.
stuck: Stuck: “How could you start? Draw it, list it, or make a table?”
List station: “Start with the smallest digit in the hundreds place. How many numbers does each digit give?”
Measure station: “Draw the three pieces. What if all three were the same? What is extra?”
Ready for more: make a puzzle card for the next pair.

say: “Siti is 4th from the front and 6th from the back. I draw the queue: 3 people in front of Siti, Siti, then 5 people behind her. 3 + 1 + 5 = 9. If I add 4 + 6 I count Siti twice, so I take 1 away: 10 − 1 = 9.”

“A logic grid: Ben does not like curry puff or popiah, so I put two crosses in Ben’s row. Only kaya toast is left, so a tick. A tick means crosses in the rest of that column, so nobody else has kaya toast.”
“A bar graph: first I read the scale. The lines go 0, 2, 4, 6, so each space is 2. A bar halfway between 6 and 8 shows 7.”

do: Ask: “How did you start? Why did you choose that?”
Ask: “Which clue did you use first? Why that one?”
Ask: “How do you know you have found ALL of them?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Draw it: put people or bars on paper.”
Hint 2: “Make a table and cross out what cannot be.”
Hint 3: “List it in order, smallest first, so you do not miss one.”

say: “Which start helped you most today: draw it, list it or make a table? Why?”
“Why do we take away 1 in a queue puzzle?”
ask: “Which start helped you most today: draw it, list it or make a table? Why?”
Open answers for the first. Queue: the person is counted from the front AND from the back, so they are counted twice; take away 1.

say: “You are real inquirers now: you notice, test, and explain why. Here is your certificate.”
Give each certificate with ONE 20-second sentence about one specific thing the child did well in the program (8 children: under 3 minutes).

p3l10-title.note: Objective: Choose a way to start a puzzle (draw it, list it, make a table), solve a logic grid with ticks and crosses, read and complete a bar graph with a scale, and explain the thinking. Heuristics taught: (1) draw it, list it or make a table to start; (2) a logic grid: a tick means crosses in the rest of its row and column. Materials: Puzzle cards for 2 stations (list, measure), digit cards 0 to 9 (or paper cards), squared paper, mini whiteboards, certificates, stamps. Online: Two stations, about 4 minutes each, with a timer on the screen for the switch. The timer is a guide, not a race: there is no rush, and a pair may pass on a station. Pairs are in pre-assigned breakout rooms (auto-move in, auto-close with a timer), and the tutor visits every room at least once. The tutor shares the next station card when the 4 minutes are up. No physical materials beyond paper. Logic grids and graphs are shared on screen and annotated together. Time plan (90 minutes, with a named 3-minute float inside talk time): opening 0 to 1.5, sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 4.5 (own paper, nobody marked, one show-me for both), warm-up game 4.5 to 7.5 (two rounds) and three quick questions 7.5 to 10.5, explore 10.5 to 27 (a Go further what-if is on the explore slide from the start; pairs go to pre-assigned breakout rooms), teaching 27 to 36.5 (how to start a puzzle: draw it, make a table, read the scale; click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 36.5 to 41.5, worksheet 41.5 to 71 (page 1 in pairs, short teaching, page 2 on their own, a 60-second self-check slide after each page; after question 3 of page 1 any child may choose Think harder or the Investigation; from minute 68 everyone chooses), talk time 71 to 77 (volunteers first, pass is fine), exit ticket 77 to 82, look back 82 to 85, stamp and close 85 to 90. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are open to every child; the tutor never announces who is on which page and invites the whole group, never one child. If the class is behind, children finish the last question of each page at home; the check slides cover it.

p3l10-warmcheck.note: Minutes 1.5 to 4.5. Sneak-peek puzzles: two small puzzles on ideas we have not learnt yet. Give about 1 minute for each puzzle, then say "show me" ONCE for both: children hold up their paper with both answers in one camera hold-up (about 30 seconds). SAY: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome and so is I do not know. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is an ACCESS puzzle: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. Children write both answers on their own paper and show them only to the tutor on camera (or everybody holds paper to the camera at the same moment, once for both puzzles). No private messages. Never answers read out, never "who got it?". Do not show the answers on the slide now. Puzzle 1 answer (tutor only): 6 orders. Listen for: ABM, AMB, BAM, BMA, MAB, MBA. Listing by who is first helps to find them all. Puzzle 2 answer (tutor only): 3 orders: ABM, BAM, BMA. Listen for: Cross out every order where Mei comes before Ben. Come back to puzzle 2 at talk time: "Now we know the idea, how could it help?" (volunteers only). Invite the WHOLE group once, never one child; this is an invitation, not a ranking, and any child may choose Think harder or the Investigation after question 3 of page 1. Never announce who is on which page, and never split pairs unless both children agree.

p3l10-warm1.note: Minutes 4.5 to 7.5. Play ONE chain through once (two short rounds at most). Relay chain, made safe: the TUTOR reads each card; volunteers say the answer (a pass is always fine, and the tutor or the group gives it). The chain never depends on one child: if an answer is wrong the tutor says "Let us check together" and writes the correct number on screen, and the chain carries on from the correct number. No child is named as the one who broke the chain. Click to show each answer after it is said. Chain: 6 × 9 = 54 (tables), 54 + 46 = 100 (adding to the next hundred), 100 × 7 = 700, 700 − 250 = 450, 450 ÷ 5 = 90 (think 45 tens ÷ 5 = 9 tens), 90 minutes = 1 h 30 min (time). Second round if time: start with 8 × 7 and change the steps.

p3l10-warm2.note: Minutes 7.5 to 10.5. One question from each part of our program. Read each aloud, give thinking time, then click. Ask "Which lesson does this remind you of?" Answers: 1) 700 (hundreds place). 2) 5/8 (add the eighths; the bottom number stays). 3) 9 remainder 2 (9 × 5 = 45, 2 left). Three quick questions only; 4) perimeter of a 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle (20 cm) and 5) 2 kg 50 g = 2050 g (not 250 g) are on the take-home box of the Go further page in the workbook.

p3l10-explore1.note: Minutes 10.5 to 22.5. Two stations only, so that the rotation fits online: each station is 4 minutes (the List station has only 6 numbers and the ribbon answers are 30, 40 and 50 cm), and 9 minutes of pair work includes the switch. Share the List card first (4 minutes), then the Measure card (4 minutes), and switch with a timer on the slide. The timer is a guide, not a race: say so out loud, do not count down aloud, and do not use words like hurry or quickly. A pair may pass on a station, or write how far they got; praise the thinking, not the speed. The debrief on the next slide is question 1 only, plus the two answers. Visit every breakout room at least once during the two stations (about 1 minute per room). Ribbon scaffold (say it if a pair is stuck, do not tell the answer): draw the ribbon as 3 boxes, the short piece, then a piece with a 10 cm extra, then a piece with a 20 cm extra; take the extras (10 + 20) away from 120 cm. Pairs stay in their pre-assigned breakout room. List: make every 3-digit number from the cards 3, 6, 9 (there are 6). Measure: a 120 cm ribbon is cut into 3 pieces, each piece 10 cm longer than the one before. Draw it and find each piece (30 cm, 40 cm, 50 cm). The graph and logic puzzles come next on worksheet page 1. Online: one station card on screen at a time, then report back. GO FURTHER (on the slide from the start of explore, so nobody waits): A 120 cm ribbon is cut into 4 pieces, each 10 cm longer than the last. How long is each? Answer: 15 cm, 25 cm, 35 cm and 45 cm (take away 10 + 20 + 30 = 60, 60 cm left, 60 / 4 = 15). Any pair may choose it as soon as their first task is done; do not say who is ready for it. Online: pairs are in pre-assigned breakout rooms (set up before the lesson, auto-move in and auto-close with a timer, about 45 seconds per move). Visit each breakout room at least once while the pairs work (about 1 minute per room).

p3l10-explore2.note: Minutes 22.5 to 27. Gather the pairs. Ask question 1 only; the two answers are on the slide (show them and let one or two pairs say how they checked). Answers: 1) Open: listen for "I drew it", "I listed them in order", "I made a table". 2) 6 numbers: 369, 396, 639, 693, 936, 963. Each hundreds digit has 2 numbers, so 3 × 2 = 6. 3) 30 cm, 40 cm and 50 cm: take away the extras (10 cm and 20 cm) from 120 cm: 90 cm, so 30 cm each; then give the extras back. Check: 30 + 40 + 50 = 120.

p3l10-teach1.note: Teach: the idea and why. "Today mixes everything. Clever inquirers do not know every answer straight away; they know how to START." Click each card and give an example from our P3 lessons: Draw it (bar models in Lesson 4, time lines in Lesson 9). List it (digit puzzles in Lesson 1, budgets in Lesson 9). Make a table (times-table patterns in Lesson 3). Click the last box and read it together. The next slides show each start in action.

p3l10-try1.note: Worked example and your turn in one slide (the old separate worked-example slide was merged here). Ask first: "Is it 10?" Many children add 4 + 6. Think-aloud: "I draw Siti. 4th from the front means 3 people are in front of her. 6th from the back means 5 people behind her. Count: 3 + 1 + 5 = 9. If I add 4 + 6, I count Siti twice, so I take 1 away." Then whiteboards. a) 1 in front, Ravi, 7 behind: 9 (or 2 + 8 − 1). b) 2 in front, Ben, so 10 − 3 = 7 behind: Ben is 8th from the back (10 − 3 + 1). c) Draw two bars: take away the extra 6: 24; share: 12 and 12; give the 6 back: 12 and 18. Check 12 + 18 = 30.

p3l10-we2.note: Worked example: make a table. (The old logic-grid try-it slide was cut; worksheet Q2 is the practice. If there is a moment, ask orally: Ali, Mei and Ben choose red, blue, green; Mei does not choose red or blue, so green; Ali does not choose red, so blue; Ben has red.) Click order: Ben’s two crosses, Ben’s tick, the crosses in the kaya toast column, the last marks; the three side notes rise in between as you talk. Think-aloud: "A table keeps every clue in one place. Clue 1 tells me 2 things Ben does NOT like: 2 crosses. Only one box is left in his row, so a tick. A tick means nobody else can have kaya toast, so I cross out the rest of that column. Clue 2: Ravi is not curry puff, and kaya toast is gone, so Ravi likes popiah. Siti gets the last one: curry puff." Check each clue against the answer.

p3l10-we3.note: Worked example: a bar graph (books borrowed from the class library). Ask first: "How many books on Tuesday?" Children who count spaces say 3 or 4. Click step 1: "Before reading any bar, read the scale. The lines go up in 2s." Step 2: "Tuesday is halfway between 6 and 8: 7." Step 3: "How many more" means the difference. Answer: add all four. The worksheet graph goes up in 10s with halfway values (5s); do not read it for them.

p3l10-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Queues: adding the two places and counting the person twice. (2) Bar graphs: counting spaces as 1 instead of reading the scale; missing the halfway values 45 and 55. (3) Logic grids: a tick without crossing out the rest of the row and column. (4) Digit cards: missing a number because the list is not in order. (5) Matchstick pattern: 4 sticks for every square (shared sticks are counted twice).

p3l10-break.note: Five minutes. Show 15:00, 18:00, 21:15, 09:30. Online: children stay in view of the camera and move in place.

p3l10-ws1.note: Minutes 41.5 to 57. Walk around. Ask "How did you start?" and "Which clue did you use first?" before helping. Q1c: they must find the missing number first (200 − 150), then draw the bar to the 50 line. Q2: if a pair is stuck, ask "Who can be in the choir?" (clue 2 and clue 1 rule out three people). PAGE 1 CLOCK (41.5 to 57): about 2 minutes to hand out and get started, then pairs auto-move to their pre-assigned breakout rooms (about 45 seconds), about 12 minutes of pair work with the room timer on, and auto-close back to the main room (about 45 seconds). Visit each room once. Items not finished are finished at home; the check slide covers them.

p3l10-ws1ans.note: Click after a pair explains. Q1: Milo 45, Teh 30, Kopi 55, Bandung 20. b) 55 − 30 = 25. c) 45 + 30 + 55 + 20 = 150; 200 − 150 = 50. d) Check all pairs: only 45 + 55 = 100. Q2: Clue 2 says Mei and Ravi are not in the choir; clue 1 says Ali is not; so Siti is in the choir. Clue 3: the swimmer has 4 letters: Ravi or Siti; Siti is in the choir, so Ravi swims. Ali: not choir, not chess, not swimming, so football. Mei: chess. The puzzle has exactly one answer. SELF-CHECK, about 60 seconds: children correct their own page against these answers in a different colour and hold the corrected page up to the camera once. Ask “how do you know?” on ONE question only. Do not go through every answer aloud.

p3l10-teachlist.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4 and Q6). Left: "I list them in order. Start with 3 in the hundreds place: 369, 396. Then 6: 639, 693. Then 9: 936, 963. Two for each first digit, so 6. Even numbers end in an even digit: only 6 is even, so 396 and 936." Right: "For a find-ALL riddle, I list every case for one clue, then cross out the ones that break another clue." The worksheet uses different digits and an odd-number riddle: do not do them here. This ONE recap slide replaces three teaching slides. Also say in one sentence each: Draw it (queues): count the person from the front AND from the back, so take away 1; Make a table (matchsticks, Q5): the first square needs 4 sticks and each new square adds 3, so keep the table going. Q3 is a page-1 question: it is in the worksheet, not here.

p3l10-ws2.note: Children work alone; there is one recap slide before page 2 (the page-1 queue question Q3 is not taught here). Note who needs a short catch-up. Q6: check that children list every case (digit sets 1, 1, 4 and 1, 2, 3; the ones digit must be odd) and cross out, not stop at the first answer.

p3l10-ws2ans.note: Click after a child explains. Q3a: 2 in front, Ben, 4 behind: 7 (3 + 5 − 1). Q3b: 1 in front of Ali, Ali, 3 between, Siti: 6. Q4: odd ones end in 5: 285 and 825. 582 is 18 from 600; 528 is 72 away. Q5: the first square needs 4 sticks, each new square adds 3 (it shares a side). 8 squares: 4 + 7 × 3 = 25. Keep the table going: 22, 25, 28, 31 at 10 squares. Q6: digits add to 6, none 0, odd: ones digit 1 (hundreds and tens add to 5: 41 or 32, hundreds bigger: 411, 321), ones 3 (add to 3: 21: 213), ones 5 (add to 1: impossible). SELF-CHECK, about 60 seconds: children correct their own page against these answers in a different colour and hold the corrected page up to the camera once. Ask “how do you know?” on ONE question only. Do not go through every answer aloud.

p3l10-stretch.note: For children who choose Think harder. Answers: 1) 145 (Mei 20 + 15 = 35; Siti 35 + 20 = 55; 35 + 20 + 35 + 55 = 145). 2) Siti: if Ben is just behind Siti, the line is Siti, Ben, Ali or Ali, Siti, Ben; Ali is not first, so Siti, Ben, Ali. 3) Day 4: make a table: end of day 1: highest point 5 m (night: slides back to 3 m), day 2: highest point 8 m (night: 6 m), day 3: highest point 11 m (night: 9 m), day 4: 9 + 5 = 14 m, past the top. Many children say day 4 because 12 ÷ 3 = 4, which is the right day but the wrong reason: check the table.

p3l10-challenge.note: Use as a pair challenge or in talk time. Ask for the reason every time. Answers: 1) 13 children (5 in front of Siti, Siti, 3 between, Ravi, 3 behind Ravi: 5 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 3 = 13). 2) 3P1 40 kg, 3P2 30 kg, 3P3 40 kg, 3P4 25 kg (compare everything with 3P2: the extras are +10, +10 and −5, so 135 − 15 = 120 kg is 4 equal parts of 30 kg).

p3l10-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried the Go further, or if they are stuck. The diagrams show the problem, not the answer. Ask: What do you know? What do you not know yet? For Q1: "Can you draw the children in front of Siti and behind Ravi?" For Q2: "Why compare with 3P2?" (every clue talks about 3P2 or 3P1). Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p3l10-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried, with the "see it" slide. Q1: the trap is to add 6 + 3 + 4 = 13 by luck or 6 + 4 + 3 + 2 by guessing; the drawing makes it sure: 5 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 3. Q2: 3P4 is 5 kg LESS than 3P2, so to make it equal we add 5 back (135 − 20 + 5 = 120). Check: 40 + 30 + 40 + 25 = 135.

p3l10-talk.note: Minutes 71 to 77. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then volunteers share (a pass is always fine, and nobody is called on by name). Ask: "Draw it, list it or make a table: which helped you most today? Why?" Teaching a puzzle to the group is only for volunteers. Also ask: "Why do we take away 1 in a queue puzzle?" (the person is counted from the front and from the back). Praise the reasons, not only the answers. TALK TIME FLOAT: this part holds the lesson's named 3-minute float. If you are behind, shorten talk time (one discussion question, then the partner share); if you are on time, use the full time for the second question and the return to sneak-peek puzzle 2. Never take time from the exit ticket, look back or stamp. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a pass is always fine and so is sharing with a partner. No cold-calling by name, no public tallies or rankings, and nobody is told they were wrong in front of the group. Nobody is called on by name.

p3l10-exit.note: Minutes 77 to 82. Answer: 7 people (3 in front, Ali, 3 behind; 4 + 4 − 1 = 7), started by drawing it. A child who writes 8 has counted Ali twice. The favourite-lesson line is open: use it to plan next steps. This is the easiest item of the lesson: allow 2 minutes of work, not 3.5. Next slide: look back (3 minutes: 2 for the children plus a short share). Extension: write a logic grid puzzle with 3 people and 3 things for a friend, and check it has exactly one answer. Answers are shown only to the tutor on camera (own paper). Never mark or read out answers in front of the group. Reflection (look back) follows on the next slide: allow 3 minutes, 2 for the children plus a short share.

p3l10-reflect.note: Minutes 82 to 85. Look back: short and safe. SAY: "Turn to the last page of today and find Look back. Tick or write one thing for each line. There are no right answers, and you may pass on any line." Give the children a full 2 minutes, then a short share (the slide has 3 minutes). The page is never collected, marked or read out in front of the group. Children keep their page. The tutor does not see the page, so say: "If something is still puzzling you, you can show this page to a grown-up at home, or tell me at the start of next lesson." At the start of the next lesson, in the open session, invite anyone who would like another look at a puzzle (volunteers only, by hand signal or in the chat; never a private message). Invite volunteers only (one or two) to share something they did well, or what helped. Praise the strategy ("you drew it and that got you unstuck"), not the speed or the answer. Then stamp the journal and close (minutes 85 to 90).

end.note: Minutes 85 to 90. Hand out certificates and stamp the journal: say each certificate in one 20-second sentence (one specific thing the child did well), about 2.7 minutes for 8 children. Ask for volunteers on "a puzzle I enjoyed" ONCE (pass is fine). Post the parent summary from the tutor guide after the lesson; do not read it out.
